li.a: CBC News: Biker gangs in Canada
Vice: How the Hells Angels Conquered Canada
Vice: How Canada's Most Prolific Hit Man Turned Informant on the Hells Angels
One Percenter Bikers: Popeyes MC (Motorcycle Club)
Radio Canada International: Les groupes de motards au Canada

content.p: The Popeyes were a French-speaking outlaw motorcycle club from Montreal's east end, described by Vice as known for "drugs, prostitution, extortion, theft". Its fights with rival clubs, as recorded by one biker-history site, involved chains, bats, knives and shotguns. Then, on 5 December 1977, its members swapped their patches for those of the Hells Angels, and the Popeyes ceased to exist under their own name. What they became was, by the account of CBC News, the largest and most feared chapter the Hells Angels had in Canada.
Much of what is told about the Popeyes comes from police sources, informants and enthusiast histories rather than from the club, so the claims below are credited to those who made them.

Nobody agrees on exactly when the Popeyes began. One biker-history site, One Percenter Bikers, says the club was founded in Canada "sometime in the 1950s", noting that some sources report 1951. Even the origin of the name is a guess: the same site says it could find no image of the club's patch, and that it was "most likely" based on the Popeye the Sailor cartoon.

What is clearer is the club's size and language. The same site says that at their height the Popeyes were thought to outnumber every other Montreal club and to rank second nationally, behind Satan's Choice. They were the largest of the French-speaking clubs. Yves Buteau, known as "le Boss", became president in the mid-1970s.

The club's income, as described by Vice, was "the usual gangster stuff: drugs, prostitution, extortion, theft". One Percenter Bikers adds that in the 1970s a family of brothers named Dubois, who held a share of the drug trade in the area, hired the Popeyes as muscle, and that under Buteau the club became a professional distribution network. Those claims are the site's own and are not supported by a court ruling on the pages consulted.
content.h2: Street fights with the Devil's Disciples
content.p: As the Popeyes grew richer, rival clubs tried to take a share. Vice names the Devil's Disciples and the Ontario-based Satan's Choice. The violence that followed, the magazine says, helped establish Quebec's reputation as one of the most dangerous places in North America for organised crime. By 1975, according to Vice, the Devil's Disciples had folded after losing 15 members to murder at the hands of one criminal group or another, without saying which.
One Percenter Bikers lists several clashes from these years:

On 1 June 1968 a fight between the two clubs, with chains and bats and an estimated 100 people involved, left many injured, four of them hospitalised. Later that month, on 17 June, eight Devil's Disciples riding on Fabre Street in Jacques Cartier were blocked by about ten Popeyes, and a knife fight followed. Five people were arrested, and an 18-year-old Devil's Disciples member, Jean-Yves Picquet, died of stab wounds. On 26 May 1969 a Popeyes member, Pierre Boucher, was stabbed to death, with 58 knife wounds, by three Devil's Disciples members, one of them named as Andre Bureau.

The site also records that on 8 July 1970 police were called to an apparent shootout, questioned 13 Popeyes at their Montreal clubhouse and found three shotguns and a machete. On 14 August 1976, Buteau and other members were arrested at a hotel in Saint-Andre-Avellion after about 50 members were involved in trashing it. The pages consulted do not give the outcome of any of these arrests, so no convictions are claimed here.
content.h2: An inside view of the violence
content.p: The fullest picture of the club's violence comes from one of its own members. Yves Trudeau joined the east-end Popeyes in 1968, at 22. Vice, drawing on the journalist and author James Dubro, describes a young man fascinated by bikers, weapons and bombs who had worked at an explosives factory. He earned the nickname "Apache" after he was reputed to have cut off the head of one victim. By the time the club joined the Hells Angels, Vice says, he had already killed four people.

Trudeau's own later admissions, as reported by Vice, are the best-known measure of what the Popeyes and their successors did. The article says he admitted to being personally involved in 43 deaths from 1970 to 1985, made up of 29 shootings, 10 bombings, three beatings and a strangling. He also took contracts from outside the club, the article says, including for the largely Irish West End Gang, which controlled the Port of Montreal. In January 1982, Vice reports, that gang's leader forced the Hells to kill three of their own members and a girlfriend, among them a founding Montreal Hells Angel and former Popeyes member, Denis Kennedy. Dubro says Trudeau pulled the trigger on Kennedy.
These are an informant's accounts, relayed by a magazine. Where the pages name a conviction, it is Trudeau's own: he later pleaded guilty to 43 charges of manslaughter.

By the mid-1970s the American clubs were looking north. Vice says the Chicago-based Outlaws and the California-based Hells Angels both wanted to expand internationally. In the summer of 1977, five of the ten Satan's Choice chapters, including the Montreal one, joined the Outlaws. The Popeyes went the other way.

The ceremony took place at a party in Laval. Len Isnor, an Ontario Provincial Police staff sergeant who runs that province's biker enforcement unit, told Vice that the Hells Angels had scouted possible Canadian partners and chose the Popeyes because of their reputation as "the most prosperous and the most violent". "They'd take on anyone. And win," he said. He added that access to the Port of Montreal and the club's existing ties to the Italian Mafia and the West End Gang were a bonus.

One Percenter Bikers says about 35 members patched over, the others being either uninterested or not up to the Angels' standard, and that the first Canadian Hells Angels chapter was based in Sorel, Quebec. It also reports, as a belief rather than established fact, that Hells Angels leader Sonny Barger approached Buteau directly, and that Buteau became the Hells Angels' Canadian president. In 1979, according to Vice, the Montreal chapter had become unwieldy and a second chapter, made up largely of ex-Popeyes, was created in Laval and known as the North Chapter, while Sorel remained the provincial mother chapter.

Timing mattered. The Outlaws had arrived in Ontario months earlier and were moving into Quebec. Vice says the two clubs fought what became known as the First Biker War from 1977 to 1982, which the Angels won. Within weeks of the patch-over, the article says, Trudeau shot a young Outlaws member outside a bar in Little Italy, his fifth killing, which it credits with sparking a full-fledged war.

One Percenter Bikers also reports that on 8 September 1983 Buteau was shot dead by Gino Goudreau, described as a 22-year-old reported to be a drug dealer, a member of a rival club, with a brother in the Outlaws. This is a single site's statement; no court outcome is given, and it is not confirmed here. The same site says Michel Langlois, a prominent ex-Popeye, then became the Hells Angels' Canadian national president.
content.h2: Lennoxville, and the people the Popeyes became
content.p: Within a few years the Laval chapter, full of former Popeyes, became a problem for its own club. According to Vice, its heavy cocaine use, flouting of club rules and disrespect toward other criminals became a serious issue, and its members were also accused of withholding profits from a sale to the West End Gang. In March 1985 the Sorel chapter declared Laval to be in "bad standing" and drew up a list of North members to be killed.

On Sunday 24 March 1985, at the Sherbrooke chapter's clubhouse in Lennoxville, the chapter's president, Laurent Viau, and four other North members were shot dead, wrapped in sleeping bags and chained to concrete blocks, and dumped in the St. Lawrence River, according to Vice. Another North chapter member, Jean-Pierre Mathieu, was found days later. The two Vice articles describe the toll slightly differently. One says five were lured and killed, with a sixth killed a couple of weeks later; the other names five men and the skeleton of a woman, the wife of a former member, hauled from the river by June, with Mathieu found separately. Trudeau, who had checked himself into a detox centre and missed the trap, was himself on the target list and later turned on the club.

In April 1985 he was picked up on a weapons charge and sentenced to a year. In prison, Vice says, he agreed to testify against his former colleagues in exchange for a better cell and a reduced sentence, and gave his first public testimony at a coroner's inquest that August. Experts quoted by the magazine say his testimony and that of two other informants led directly to about 19 Hells Angels being convicted, four of them directly connected to Lennoxville. He pleaded guilty to 43 charges of manslaughter and served seven years, a deal that Conservative senator Pierre-Hugues Boisvenu called an example of abuse of the system. After release in 1994 he was given a new identity, and in 2004 he was re-arrested on a sexual assault charge involving a boy under 14, to which he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to four years.

The Lennoxville killings, Vice says, laid the seeds of the Second Biker War. According to that article, Salvatore Cazzetta, angered that the Angels had killed their own members, founded the Rock Machine in 1986 with his brother. CBC and Radio Canada International say the Rock Machine emerged in 1986 and became the Hells Angels' biggest rival, and that the turf war that followed in the 1990s cost more than 150 lives. Among the dead were two prison guards and a boy of 11, Daniel Desrochers, killed by a car bomb outside a biker hangout. Vice puts the figure at about 160 by 2002. His death and the public anger prompted Bill C-95, passed in 1997, which stiffened penalties for people convicted of crimes while members of established criminal organisations.

By 2009, CBC reported, the Hells Angels were estimated to have 34 chapters and about 460 full members across Canada, according to Criminal Intelligence Service Canada. That year a police sweep known as Operation SharQc led to 156 arrests, though Vice notes that many of the charges were later thrown out because of delays that breached defendants' Charter rights.

The Popeyes themselves never returned. CBC says only that the Montreal chapter opened in 1977 "when a biker gang called the Popeyes joined the Angels", and Radio Canada International that the club "scuttled itself" to do so. The club's name survives mainly in the histories of the men who wore its patch, and in the contested numbers of those who died in the wars that followed.
